notes: How this game's places are lit.
The settings screen says what you want everywhere. This file says what a
particular place wants, and where it gives an answer, that answer is the
one in force there. Which file is in force is chosen on the settings
screen, under Game config; choose None, or take this file out of the
folder, and every map falls back to the settings alone.
As it ships this file changes nothing. It states no value and names no
map, so the picture is exactly the settings screen's own. Everything
below is here to be read and filled in.
JSON has no comments, so anything written under a key called "notes" is
the documentation: at any level, as one line or as a list of them, and
never read as data. It is a reserved name that no part of this file will
ever use for anything else.
A file that is not JSON at all costs the whole file -- one missing brace
moves every following line into a different place, so nothing is loaded
and whatever was in force stays in force. Anything else costs only
itself: an unknown key, a value out of range or a colour that is not six
hexadecimal digits is reported, that key is ignored, and the rest of the
file is read.
Angles are in degrees. Distances are in world units. EVERY NUMBER IN
EVERY TABLE BELOW IS DECIMAL, and every one of them is a number the ROTH
Editor prints for the same thing: write what is on your screen.
What every map gets, including the maps nobody lists below.
"settings" holds settings-screen keys, spelled exactly as the settings
file spells them and read by exactly the same rules -- so every bound
and every complaint comes from the settings screen itself, and the two
can never disagree. A key belongs here when it says how a PLACE is lit
rather than what a SCREEN wants: the shading and the whole light rig
may be written here, and the brightness and contrast of the picture may
not. For example:
"settings": {
"shading_mode": "modern",
"room_light_reach": 0.85,
"player_light_intensity": 0.4,
"player_light_flicker": true,
"ambient_color": "#576180"
THE ONE-GLANCE RULE, before anything else. Select a thing in the ROTH
Editor and read its Lighting field: 0 means the game already lights the
room with it, and anything else means the game draws it as an ordinary
object. A GRANT MAKES EITHER OF THEM A LIGHT. Naming the first tunes a
light that is already there; naming the second creates one, and the
thing is then DRAWN lit as well, the way the map's own lights are.
THE COLOUR IS OPTIONAL EVERYWHERE THERE IS A PICTURE TO READ IT OFF. A
thing is drawn with a picture and a surface is painted with one, so
leave the colour out and it is taken from that picture: a torch throws
its own flame's colour and a ward its own. Only "placed" below has no
picture of any kind, and only "placed" therefore requires a colour.
SHADOWS ARE A COUNT ON THE SETTINGS SCREEN, and every light follows
it unless an entry here says otherwise: the few lights lighting most
of what the player can see cast real shadows, and the rest light the
room without one. Writing "shadows": true on a light PINS it -- it
casts wherever it stands in that ranking, which is how to say that
THIS lamp is the one that matters in this room -- and it spends one
of the count's own places rather than coming free. "shadows": false
refuses a light shadows, and refuses one a broader entry pinned. A
count of nought turns them all off, pinned lights included.
"lights" holds five tables. Two are blankets over a whole game and may
be written here; the other three name particular things in one map and
belong under "maps" below.
"sprites" says what a KIND of thing gives off, keyed by EITHER of the
two numbers the editor prints for one picture: the TEXTURE INDEX and
TEXTURE SOURCE pair its object panel shows for a selected object,
written "34/0", or the single PICTURE NUMBER its picking window shows,
written "4130". They are the same key -- see the note under the table
below. Use it for where one value for a whole map is not enough, such as
a brazier that should read brighter than a table candle. Nothing has to
be listed for a map's torches to work: the game already marks them,
custom maps included.
"lights": {
"sprites": {
"colour": "#ffb46e" },
Every one of those three is real on the first study map: 34/0 is the
lit torch, 112/0 an arcane wall ward the map does NOT light, and 93/0
the EMPTY candelabra -- which is what the third line is for. The middle
line is the whole ruling in one: it names a thing the map never lit, it
states no colour, and it makes every ward of that kind a light of its
own colour, drawn lit. Each field stands on its own, so a map may raise
a strength without restating a colour. "off" is the whole entry rather
than a field: a thing that is plainly not a light -- an empty
candlestick, a glowing decal, a bright pickup -- is refused outright.
"lit" says whether the thing itself is DRAWN lit, the way the map's own
lights are. Say nothing and it is -- that is what a grant has always
done, and what keeps a torch from reading as a dark sprite with a halo
round it. Write "lit": false to keep the ordinary shading on the sprite
while the light it gives stands: the thing is then lit by the lights
around it, its own among them, glowing with its own light rather than
painted bright. It belongs to "sprites" and "objects" alone -- textures
and faces grant surfaces, and a placed light is drawn by nothing -- and
on a thing the map itself lights (Lighting 0 in the editor) the mark is
the map's own statement, which this field does not unmark.
THE TWO NUMBERS FOR ONE PICTURE. The editor's object panel shows a
Texture Index and a Texture Source; its picking window shows one number
instead, which is that picture's own place in the DAS FILE it lives in.
A map's own DAS file holds its object pictures from 4096, and the shared
DAS file holds its own from 0, so:
Texture Source 0  ->  4096 + Texture Index
Texture Source 1  ->  4352 + Texture Index
Texture Source 2  ->     0 + Texture Index
Texture Source 3  ->   256 + Texture Index
"112/0" and "4208" are therefore one key and one picture, and both may
be written.
A KEY IS A SLOT IN A FILE OF PICTURES, and that is worth knowing before
writing one HERE. Numbers in 0..511 -- Texture Source 2 and 3 -- are the
shared DAS file's, which every map loads, so a line here naming one is
exactly what it looks like: that picture, everywhere. Numbers in
4096..4607 -- Sources 0 and 1 -- and EVERY TEXTURE NUMBER are slots in
the map's OWN DAS file, and the maps of this game are dealt out of five
different ones, so a line here naming one grants whatever occupies that
slot on each map rather than one picture. Where that is not what was
meant, the "das" section below is the tool: it names the file, so the
slot is a picture again.
Under the same "lights", "textures" says what a PAINTED SURFACE gives
off -- lava, a glowing rune, a lit sigil on a wall -- keyed by the
texture number the map's own geometry carries. It covers every face and
every flat: a wall's three bands, a room's floor and ceiling, and the
two faces of a block standing in a room. It belongs here as readily as
under a map: a texture is the same texture wherever it is painted, so a
game whose lava glows usually wants it to glow everywhere.
"lights": {
"textures": {
"100": { "colour": "#7fe0a0", "strength": 1.2,
"reach": 640 }
That number is real too: 100 is the texture the sigil room's walls of
the first study map are painted with, so the line above is one you can
write, run and see -- every room carrying that texture picks up a green
light. Put your own game's lava number in its place.
Leave the colour out and it is read off the texture's own BRIGHT PART:
every texel at least half as bright as the brightest texel in the
picture, weighted by brightness. That law rather than a plain average,
because a wall is not cut out of anything the way a sprite is -- every
texel of it is the surface, so an average over lava answers with the
colour of the rock the lava is set in. Read this way, lava throws its
glow, a cold rune throws its line, and a surface painted one flat
colour throws that colour. A texture whose picture cannot be read at
all lights nothing and says so.
A TEXTURE IS NOT A SPRITE. This table is keyed by what a SURFACE is
painted with; "sprites" above is keyed by the picture an OBJECT is
drawn with. Writing a pair like "112/0" here, or a picture number like
"4208", names nothing a wall can be painted with -- and the game says
so by name rather than leaving the line quiet.
A grant lights the room; it does not repaint the surface. Whether a
face is drawn fullbright stays what the map itself says. One light is
placed per room per texture, in the middle of that room's granted faces
and just clear of them, so a lake of lava is one light over the lake
rather than three hundred fighting for the few slots the picture
carries.
THE SKY'S OWN LIGHT is described by "environment_lighting", beside
"settings" and "lights" rather than inside either. It is the one light
in the game that is not in the room with you: it comes down out of the
sky, enters wherever the map is open to it, and everything between it
and the floor -- roofs, walls, window bars, the tree outside -- casts a
shadow. A map with no opening to the sky is not touched by any of this,
so a sealed cellar needs no entry at all.
"environment_lighting": {
"colour": "#ffede0",
"strength": 0.8,
"elevation": 45
The fields, and what leaving one out means:
"on"              absent means AUTOMATIC: lit wherever the map has an
opening to the sky. Write false to hold it out of a
map that has one and should not be lit through it.
"kind"            "sun" or "moon". A LABEL: it decides which word the
light is called by and nothing else. The colour and
the strength are what it actually looks like.
"colour"          what colour the light from the sky is.
"strength"        how much of it there is.
"elevation"       how high it stands above the horizon, in DEGREES.
Low means long shadows reaching deep through side
windows; high means short ones under things.
"direction"       which way it stands over the map, in DEGREES as a
compass bearing: 0 north (the top of the map as the
editor draws it), 90 east, 180 south, 270 west. THIS
IS THE PER-MAP FIELD -- see "maps" below.
"object_shadows"  whether things standing in the world cast into it.
"shadow_quality"  "low", "medium" or "high".
"sky_ceilings"    which ceilings are open to the sky, for a map the
game reads wrongly. See below.
EVERY ONE OF THOSE IS ALSO A SETTINGS KEY, and that is worth knowing
rather than hiding: "direction" is the settings key "sun_yaw_deg",
"colour" is "sun_color", and so on down. They are one statement written
two ways, they land in the same place, and the block is simply the
friendlier spelling. Write a value both ways in one place and the block
is the answer in force, and the game says so once.
"sky_ceilings" IS THE ONE PLACE COMPOSITION IS NOT FIELD BY FIELD. It is
a list, and a list is one answer rather than a bag of fields, so a map's
list REPLACES the one above it instead of adding to it -- which is what
lets a map take a ceiling OUT of the reading as well as put one in. It
is an escape hatch and most maps want no part of it: the game reads a
ceiling as open sky when its texture number is 0 or 1, which is how the
maps of this game say it. Write the list only where that reading is
wrong for one map, and write every ceiling that IS open in it, including
0 and 1 if they still are. An empty list says that none of them is.
Running the game with HWR_OBJ_DUMP set to a file name writes out every
object a map DRAWS: its own number in the first column, then where it
stands, then the sprite pair it is drawn with and the ID its creator
gave it -- all decimal, and all the same numbers the ROTH
Editor shows for the same object. After those come the numbers of the
records the map holds and never draws, which is what an entry naming
one of them is told about by name. See "maps" below: one particular
object, one particular face and one hand-hung light are described under
the map they belong to, never here.
ONE LINE FOR A WHOLE PART OF THE GAME.
A map's pictures are not its own: every map reads them out of a DAS FILE
it shares with the other maps of its part of the game, and this game
keeps five of those plus one shared file that every map loads. So the
torch that hangs in the water halls hangs in FIFTEEN maps, and
describing it under each of them is fifteen lines to keep in step by
hand.
This is that one line. Keyed by the name of a DAS file, matched exactly
as a map's name is -- whatever its case, with or without the folder and
with or without the extension -- so DEMO1, demo1 and M\DEMO1.DAS are
one file:
"das": {
"DEMO1": {
"notes": "The fifteen water and cathedral maps.",
"lights": {
"sprites": { "34/0": { "strength": 1.8,
"colour": "#ffb46e" } },
"textures": { "2609": { "strength": 1.2, "reach": 640 } }
That entry is in force on every map whose pictures come out of
DEMO1.DAS and on no other map. This game's own files, which is the
table to write against:
DEMO    CAVERNS, OPTEMP1, STUDY1, STUDY2, STUDY3, STUDY4, TEMPLE1
DEMO1   AQUA1, AQUA2, CHURCH1, ELOHIM1, LRINTH, LRINTH1, RAQUIA1 to
RAQUIA5, SOULST2, SOULST3, VICAR, VICAR1
DEMO2   ANUBIS, GNARL1, TGATE1F to TGATE1I, TOWER1
DEMO3   ABAGATE2, DOMINION, DOPPLE, SALVAT
DEMO4   AELF, CAVERNS2, CAVERNS3, GRAVE, MAS3, MAS4, MAS6, MAS7,
MAUSO1EA, MAUSO1EB, MAZE
ADEMO   every map: it is the shared file, and naming it is how to say
everywhere and mean it
THE THREE SCOPES COMPOSE LEAST SPECIFIC FIRST, field by field, by the
one rule everything here composes by:
"everywhere" -> the shared DAS file -> the map's own DAS file -> the
map
so a map's own line beats what its DAS file says, which beats what every
place gets, and "off" comes whole from the most specific scope naming a
thing.
ONLY THE TWO TABLES KEYED BY A PICTURE may be written in one:
"sprites" and "textures". A file of pictures is not a place and it is
not a map, so "objects", "faces" and "placed" -- numbers in one map's
own lists -- belong under a map, and "settings" and
"environment_lighting" -- how somewhere is lit -- belong under
"everywhere" or under a map. Each of those written here costs its own
key, is told where it belongs, and leaves the rest of the section
standing.
WHICH PICTURES A SECTION MAY SPEAK ABOUT is what the scope means, since
a section names a file and its keys are that file's own slots. Under a
map's OWN DAS file everything is at home: Sources 0 and 1 and every
texture number are that file's slots, and a SHARED picture ("68/2", or
0..511) is kept too -- the shared file is loaded on those maps as well,
so such a line is that picture scoped to the maps this file is dealt to.
Under the SHARED file, ADEMO, only its own pictures mean anything: a key
naming one of the map's own slots names a different picture on every map
that loads a different file, so it is left out and the game says so
once, naming how many.
A SECTION NAMING NO DAS FILE THE GAME HOLDS says so once, rather than
sitting there quietly doing nothing -- which is what a map's name
written here by mistake gets. A section naming a real file that a
particular map does not load stays silent, because that is the whole
point of the scope.
One entry per place, keyed by the name of the map's OWN file, without
the folder and without the extension: STUDY1, CRYPT1, TOWER1. The name
is matched whatever its case and with or without an extension, so
"study1" and "STUDY1.RAW" name one map. Maps that share a DAS file are
still different maps here -- what they share is described under "das"
above. A map nobody lists gets "everywhere" alone, silently, so a map
pack is covered whether or not anyone has described it.
A map's entry has the SAME shape as "everywhere" above, and that is the
whole of the composition rule: a map's answer is laid over the game's
answer, field by field.
"STUDY1": {
"notes": "Lamplit and enclosed; its own candles carry it.",
"settings": { "room_light_reach": 0.72 },
"lights": { "sprites": { "34/0": { "strength": 2.0 } } }
A row a map answers for is marked on the settings screen with what the
map says, because moving that setting will not change the picture where
you are standing.
Under "lights" a map may also describe ONE PARTICULAR OBJECT of it
rather than a kind of them -- the candelabra in one room, not every
candelabra in the game. Each entry names its object THE WAY THE ROTH
EDITOR NAMES IT, so the numbers you write are the numbers you are
reading off your screen while you write them. Two ways, and an entry
uses exactly one:
"index": N   the object's own number, which the editor shows as
"Object: N" when you select it. It names one thing.
"id": N      the number the editor shows as "ID:", which the map's
creator typed to gather objects into a group for the
command system. It is MEANT to be shared, so this
applies to every object with that ID -- which is how a
whole set of wards is tuned in one line. An ID of 0 is
refused: it is the default that most objects carry.
"STUDY1": {
"lights": {
"objects": [
{ "notes": "the standing candelabra the map never lit",
"index": 70,
"colour": "#ffb46e",
"strength": 1.4, "reach": 420 },
{ "notes": "every arcane ward given one ID by its author",
{ "notes": "a lit torch that is one too many here",
"index": 250, "off": true }
Every number there is real. On STUDY1 object 70 is the standing
candelabra of a small room and its Lighting reads 128, so the map does
NOT light it -- naming it is what turns it into a light, and the colour
on that entry is a choice rather than a requirement. The ID 36 is
carried by nine arcane wall wards, six of which the map does light and
three of which it does not: one line reaches all nine, tunes the six
and makes the other three, each throwing the colour of its own picture.
Objects 247 to 250 are the map's four lit torches, which the map lights
already and which carry no ID at all, so a torch is addressed by its
number.
What one entry says wins over whatever "sprites" said about its kind,
and an "index" entry wins over an "id" entry -- the most specific
statement anybody made is the one in force -- and all three compose
field by field, so one candelabra may be made stronger than the group
it shares an ID with without restating the colour its kind already has.
"off" is the whole entry here too: turning one object off leaves every
other object of its kind and its group alight, and naming one object in
a map whose whole kind is "off" makes that one a light again.
NUMBERS MOVE WHEN A MAP IS EDITED. An object's number is its position
in the map's own list, so deleting an object in the editor shifts the
number of every object after it. For a finished map "index" is exact
and stable; for a map still being built the ID is the stable handle,
because it travels with the object it was typed on.
An entry that addresses NOTHING says so, once, naming the map: a number
nothing answers to, a record the map holds and never draws, a number
past the end of the map's own list, an ID nothing carries, and -- for
"sprites" written under a map -- a picture nothing there is drawn with.
A mistyped number is visible rather than quietly doing nothing.
Under the same "lights", "faces" names ONE FACE of the map's own
geometry, and it is the same pair again because the editor shows the
same pair for a face:
"index": N   the face's own number, which the editor shows as
"Face: N" when you select a wall. It names one face.
"id": N      the read-only "Face ID" beside it, which is the handle
the map's command system addresses a face by. One
texture-mapping record may be shared by several faces,
so this names a group of them. An ID of 0 is refused:
it is what a face with none of its own reads as.
"STUDY1": {
"lights": {
"faces": [
{ "notes": "the wall the north room's sigil hangs on",
"colour": "#7fe0a0", "strength": 0.8 }
Face 2430 of STUDY1 is a wall of the sigil room, painted with texture
100 and carrying the Face ID 11. A named face keeps a light of its OWN,
at the middle of that face pushed just clear of it, rather than being
averaged into the middle of the room with the rest -- and a face named
"off" is taken out of its room's blanket as well. What a named face
says is laid over whatever "textures" already said about the texture it
is painted with, so a face may be made stronger without restating that
colour. A face has no Lighting field of its own, so a named face always
emits; where nothing in that composition states a colour, one is read
off the texture the face is actually painted with, by the same
bright-part law a texture grant uses.
And under the same "lights", "placed" hangs a light that belongs to
NO object at all, at three numbers you choose because there is nothing
standing there to tune:
"STUDY1": {
"lights": {
"placed": [
{ "notes": "a lamp over the stairwell",
"colour": "#ffb46e",
"strength": 1.2, "reach": 420 }
"at" and "colour" are both required. The three numbers are THE GAME'S
OWN -- the same ones HWR_OBJ_DUMP prints for the objects around them,
which is the easiest way to find a sensible one. If you take a position
off the ROTH Editor's position boxes instead, FLIP THE SIGN OF X: the
editor displays X negated. Y and Z agree.
This is the one table where the colour is required, and the reason is
that it is the one table with no picture behind it. A torch has a
sprite and lava has a texture; a light hanging in the air has neither,
so an entry without a colour lights nothing and says so.
"strength" and "reach" fall to the settings screen where they are left
out. There is no "off": an entry here exists only because you wrote it,
so delete the line.
Each one is placed in whichever of the map's rooms contains the point,
which is the same question the editor asks when you drop an object into
a room, and is then held by the same containments as every other light.
One hung outside every room lights nothing and says so.
All three lists belong to ONE map and are written under it, never
under "everywhere" and never under a DAS file: an object's number and a
face's number are numbers in one map's own lists, and the same three
numbers in another map are a different corner of a different building.
AIMING THE SKY'S OWN LIGHT IS PER-MAP WORK, and this is where it is
done. These maps were built with no sun in them at all, so which of a
map's openings catch the light is nobody's truth and everybody's
choice: stand in the room, turn "direction" until the light falls where
you want it, and write that number down here.
"TOWER1": {
"notes": "Night, high up. Moonlight through the north openings.",
"environment_lighting": {
"kind": "moon",
"colour": "#b9c8ff",
"strength": 0.35,
"elevation": 22,
"direction": 210,
"shadow_quality": "high"
Each field is laid over the game-wide answer on its own, so a map that
only turns the light round writes only "direction" and keeps the colour
and the strength every other map has. A map that should not be lit
through its openings at all writes { "on": false } and nothing else.
"CRYPT1": { "environment_lighting": { "on": false } }
And where the game reads a map's roof wrongly -- a ceiling painted with
an ordinary texture that is meant to be open air, or the other way about
-- the map names the ceilings that ARE open, and that list replaces the
reading whole rather than adding to it:
"TOWER1": {
"environment_lighting": { "sky_ceilings": [1, 2609] }
